subject: math

unit.title: Calculation: add, subtract, multiply, divide
unit.essentialQuestion: How do we add and take away bigger numbers, and what does 'lots of' mean?

title: Division as sharing and grouping
objectives: By the end, I can divide by sharing equally and by making equal groups.

vocabulary.definition: split a number into equal parts
deal one-to-each, round and round, until everything is gone
divide by making equal-sized bundles and counting the bundles
exactly the same amount in every part
vocabulary.example: every plate gets 4 — no plate gets more

emphasize: Division means FAIR, EQUAL shares — deal one-to-each like cards until they're gone. Share, don't guess.
Division has two faces: sharing ('20 between 5 — how many each?') and grouping ('how many 5s in 20?') — same fact, two stories.

keyConcepts: division as the inverse of multiplication
misconceptions: counting the total then guessing the share instead of dealing one-to-each
making unequal piles and calling it sharing
muddling sharing and grouping — not seeing they give the same division fact
not connecting ÷ to the times-table fact that solves it
hooks: 20 sweets, 5 friends — how do we share them so it's totally fair, with no tears?

plan.goal: Set up the fairness problem — 20 sweets, 5 friends; retrieve 4 × 5 from Lesson 10.
plan.note: Let the child propose a method before any teaching. The emotional stake — 'or there'll be tears!' — carries the lesson.
plan.successCriteria: Child suggests a way to share fairly and answers 4 × 5 = 20.

script.say: Big problem! I've got 20 sweets, and 5 friends are coming over. We have to share them so it's totally FAIR — no one gets more than anyone else, or there'll be tears! How would YOU make sure it's fair? … Interesting! Hold that thought. Quick memory check first: what is 4 × 5?
script.adaptHints: Swap sweets for a treat the child loves; swap friends for their real friends' names or favourite characters. Listen for 20; if shaky, skip-count 5, 10, 15, 20 together.

blocks.caption: 20 sweets, 5 friends — how do we make it FAIR?

stuckProtocol: If 4 × 5 is shaky: skip-count together in 5s — 5, 10, 15, 20 — four jumps.

plan.goal: Model fair sharing: deal one-to-each across 5 plates until gone; read the answer from one plate; link to 4 × 5 = 20.
plan.note: The dealing rhythm is the method — 'one, one, one, one, one… round again'. Then write 20 ÷ 5 = 4 and connect it to multiplication.
plan.successCriteria: Child watches the full deal, sees every plate holds 4, and hears '20 ÷ 5 = 4 — the opposite of 4 × 5 = 20'.

script.say: To share fairly, I deal one to each plate — like dealing cards. Watch: one, one, one, one, one… that's every plate with one. Round again… and again… and again… until they're ALL gone. Now every plate has exactly the same — count one plate with me: 1, 2, 3, 4. Four each! So 20 shared between 5 is 4 each: 20 ÷ 5 = 4. And look at this — that's the OPPOSITE of 4 × 5 = 20! Division undoes multiplication.
script.adaptHints: Deal with a steady rhythm the child can chant along to. Land hard on 'until they're all gone' — that's the stopping rule.

plan.goal: Division's other face — grouping: how many 5s in 20? The child makes the groups and counts THE GROUPS.
plan.note: Same 20, same answer, different story: now we bundle into 5s and count bundles. Land the punchline: sharing and grouping both write 20 ÷ 5 = 4.
plan.successCriteria: Child makes 4 groups of 5 and says 'four 5s in 20 — so 20 ÷ 5 = 4 again'.

script.say: Now the OTHER way to divide — grouping. Same 20 sweets, but this time no plates: we make bags of 5 instead. You be the bag-packer: grab 5… that's one bag. Another 5… two bags. Keep going — how many bags of 5 can you make from 20? … Four bags! So there are four 5s in 20. Write it: 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Whoa — the SAME fact! Sharing between 5 or making bags of 5 — division tells both stories.
script.adaptHints: Pause while the child 'packs' each group. If they count sweets instead of bags at the end, point: 'count the BAGS, not the sweets.'

blocks.caption: Bags of 5 — count the bags: 4. So 20 ÷ 5 = 4

blocks.prompt: How many groups of 5 can you make from 20?

wrongAnswers.why: counted the sweets in one group instead of counting the groups
wrongAnswers.remedy: You counted what's INSIDE a bag. How many BAGS did you pack?

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted 5 from 20 — read ÷ as −
wrongAnswers.remedy: We're not taking 5 away once — we're asking how many 5s FIT. Pack them: 5, 10, 15, 20 — how many bags was that?

plan.goal: Reveal whether the child deals fairly or guesses; probe the link to multiplication.
plan.note: The key diagnostic: a guessed answer (usually '5' because 5 friends) means the child never dealt. Always probe the 4 × 5 link after a correct answer.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 4 each and connects it to 4 × 5 = 20.

script.say: Your turn, fair dealer! Share 20 equally between 5 — how many does each one get? Deal them out in your head, or watch my plates if you like. … And here's my detective question: how does your answer link to 4 × 5?
script.adaptHints: If the child answers instantly and correctly, probe the inverse link. If they hesitate, replay the dealing animation slowly.

blocks.prompt: Share 20 equally between 5 — how many each?
options: 4 each — deal one-to-each until they're gone
blocks.explain: Deal one to each plate, round and round, until all 20 are gone — every plate holds 4. 20 ÷ 5 = 4, because 4 × 5 = 20.

check.question: Share 20 equally between 5 — how many each?
check.expectedAnswer: 4 (and it links to 4 × 5 = 20 — division undoes multiplication)

wrongAnswers.why: counted the total then guessed — echoed the number of friends without dealing
wrongAnswers.remedy: Deal one to each plate like cards — keep going until they're gone. NOW count one plate.

wrongAnswers.why: didn't share one-to-each — piles drifted unequal
wrongAnswers.remedy: Each round, every plate gets exactly one before any plate gets two. Try again, slowly.

plan.goal: Independent sharing AND grouping with the multiplication link named each time.
plan.note: Director draws from the practiceBank, start level 2. Alternate sharing items and grouping items so both faces stay alive. After each correct answer, ask for the matching × fact.
plan.successCriteria: Child solves 3+ divisions including one sharing, one grouping, and one linked to a times-table fact.

script.say: Practice time, fair dealer! Some questions are sharing — deal one-to-each. Some are grouping — pack the bags and count them. And after every answer, tell me the times-table fact hiding underneath. Ready to deal?
script.adaptHints: Frame shares with the child's interests (team kits, party bags, game cards). Never change the numbers.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'the sharing wasn't one-to-each' or 'we counted the wrong thing — bags, not sweets.'
Go concrete: deal the counters onto plates together on the whiteboard, one at a time.
One hint: 'Every plate gets one before any plate gets two.'
Re-ask smaller: share 6 between 3, then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child names the two faces of division and the inverse link; end on an earned win.
plan.note: Child-led recall; the character listens and only fills gaps.
plan.successCriteria: Child says division is 'sharing and grouping' and that it 'undoes multiplication'.

script.say: Tell me the two ways we can divide… and how division links to your times tables. … Yes! Sharing one-to-each, or grouping into bags — and every division is a times-table fact walking backwards. You dealt fairly one-to-each instead of guessing — that's exactly how division works.
script.adaptHints: Praise the observed process: dealing without guessing, counting the groups not the contents, naming the inverse fact.

block.prompt: Share 6 strawberries between 3 friends. How many each?
block.explain: Deal one-to-each: one round gives everyone 1, a second round gives everyone 2 — all gone. 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

wrongAnswers.why: echoed the number of friends instead of dealing
wrongAnswers.remedy: Don't guess — deal! One each… round again… are they gone? Count one pile.

wrongAnswers.why: gave the whole amount to each
wrongAnswers.remedy: There are only 6 altogether — they must be SPLIT. Deal one to each friend and see.

hints: Deal one to each friend, then round again.
Stop when they're all gone — then count ONE pile.

reteach.say: Watch the deal: one, one, one — every friend has 1. Round again: one, one, one — every friend has 2, and the strawberries are gone. 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

wrongAnswers.why: took 2 away instead of sharing — read ÷ as −
wrongAnswers.remedy: We're not taking 2 away — we're splitting 8 into 2 equal plates. Deal one-to-each and count a plate.

wrongAnswers.why: echoed the divisor
wrongAnswers.remedy: The 2 is how many PLATES. Deal all 8 out — how many land on each plate?

hints: Deal one to each plate, round and round.
8 ÷ 2 is also half of 8.

reteach.say: Two plates. Deal: one, one… two, two… three, three… four, four — gone! Each plate has 4. Splitting between 2 is the same as halving: half of 8 is 4.

block.prompt: Share 12 stickers between 3 friends. How many each?

wrongAnswers.why: echoed the number of friends — guessed without dealing
wrongAnswers.remedy: Deal one to each friend, round and round, until all 12 are gone. Now count one friend's pile.

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted 3 from 12 — read ÷ as −
wrongAnswers.remedy: Sharing isn't taking away. Split ALL 12 fairly between the 3 — deal them out.

hints: Deal one-to-each until all 12 are gone.
Which times-table fact makes 12 with a 3? 3 × ? = 12.

reteach.say: Deal 12 between 3: one each — that's 3 gone. Again — 6 gone. Again — 9 gone. Once more — all 12 gone, and everyone has 4. 12 ÷ 3 = 4, because 4 × 3 = 12.

block.prompt: Party bags! How many bags of 2 can you fill from 10 balloons?

wrongAnswers.why: counted what's inside one bag instead of counting the bags
wrongAnswers.remedy: Each bag holds 2 — but how many BAGS did you fill? Count the bags.

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted 2 from 10 — read ÷ as −
wrongAnswers.remedy: We're not taking 2 away once — we keep packing 2s until the balloons run out. Count in 2s: 2, 4, 6… how many bags?

hints: Pack 2 at a time and count the BAGS.
Count in 2s up to 10 — how many jumps?

reteach.say: Pack them: 2 balloons — one bag. 4 — two bags. 6 — three. 8 — four. 10 — five bags, balloons all gone! There are five 2s in 10, so 10 ÷ 2 = 5.

block.explain: Count in tens to 20: 10, 20 — two jumps. There are two 10s in 20.

wrongAnswers.why: echoed the divisor
wrongAnswers.remedy: The 10 is the size of each group. How many groups of 10 fit inside 20? Count: 10… 20.

wrongAnswers.why: added instead of divided
wrongAnswers.remedy: Dividing makes the number smaller or keeps it equal — never bigger. How many 10s fit in 20?

hints: Count in 10s until you reach 20.
10 and another 10 — how many is that?

reteach.say: How many 10s hide inside 20? Skip-count and keep a finger up for each: 10 — one finger. 20 — two fingers. Two 10s! 20 ÷ 10 = 2, because 2 × 10 = 20.

wrongAnswers.why: grabbed the divisor from the fact instead of the missing partner
wrongAnswers.remedy: The ÷ 5 already used the 5. Which OTHER number in 4 × 5 = 20 is the answer?

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted 5 from 20 — read ÷ as −
wrongAnswers.remedy: No need to work anything out — the times-table fact already tells you. 4 × 5 = 20 walking backwards is 20 ÷ 5 = …?

hints: Division is the times-table fact walking backwards.
? × 5 = 20 — what's the ?

reteach.say: Multiplication and division are a two-way street. 4 × 5 = 20 drives forwards; 20 ÷ 5 = 4 drives back along the SAME road. If you know one, you know the other — no new work!

block.prompt: From 3 × 10 = 30, match each question to its answer.

wrongAnswers.why: expects both divisions to give the same answer
wrongAnswers.remedy: One fact, two divisions: split 30 into 3s and you get lots of groups; split it into 10s and you get few. Which is which?

hints: One × fact gives you TWO ÷ facts.
30 ÷ 3 asks: how many 3s in 30? Skip-count in 3s… or use the fact!

reteach.say: Meet the fact family! 3, 10 and 30 live in one house. 3 × 10 = 30, 10 × 3 = 30, 30 ÷ 10 = 3, 30 ÷ 3 = 10 — four facts, one family. Learn the ×, get both ÷s free.

block.prompt: Sam works out 15 ÷ 5 by sharing 15 between 5 plates. Mia works it out by making groups of 5 and counting them. Who gets the right answer?
block.sample: Both! Sharing gives 3 on each plate; grouping gives 3 groups. 15 ÷ 5 = 3 either way — two stories, one fact.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Both — sharing and grouping both give 15 ÷ 5 = 3

wrongAnswers.why: thinks sharing and grouping are different maths with different answers
wrongAnswers.remedy: Try both with 15 counters: 5 plates gives 3 each; bags of 5 gives 3 bags. Same 3! Why do you think that happens?

wrongAnswers.answer: Neither — you have to use take-away
wrongAnswers.why: division not trusted; falls back to subtraction
wrongAnswers.remedy: Both methods split 15 into EQUAL parts — that's exactly what ÷ means. Deal it or bag it and count.

hints: Try both ways with 15 counters — compare the answers.
Sharing counts what's ON a plate; grouping counts the BAGS.

reteach.say: Division is one machine with two doors. Door one: share 15 between 5 plates — 3 each. Door two: pack 15 into bags of 5 — 3 bags. Different doors, same room: 15 ÷ 5 = 3. That's why one fact answers both kinds of question.

block.prompt: Tricky one! Share 13 biscuits fairly between 4 friends. What happens?
block.sample: Everyone gets 3, and there's 1 biscuit left over — 13 isn't a multiple of 4, so the share isn't exact.

wrongAnswers.why: rounded up — dealt a biscuit that isn't there
wrongAnswers.remedy: Deal it out for real: 4, 8, 12… can you do a whole round with only 1 biscuit left?

wrongAnswers.answer: give the last one to one friend
wrongAnswers.why: broke the fairness rule to make it come out neat
wrongAnswers.remedy: Then one friend has more — is that fair? What could we do with the spare so nobody grumbles?

hints: Deal in rounds of 4: 4 gone, 8 gone, 12 gone… what's left?
A full round needs 4 biscuits. Is 1 enough for a round?

reteach.say: Deal 13 between 4: one round uses 4 — that's 4 gone. Another — 8. Another — 12, and everyone has 3. One biscuit left, but a fair round needs 4! So it's 3 each with 1 left over. Mathematicians call that spare the remainder — you'll meet it properly later.

block.prompt: You have 4 shoes. How many PAIRS (groups of 2) is that?
block.explain: Group them in 2s: 2 shoes — one pair; 4 shoes — two pairs. 4 ÷ 2 = 2.

wrongAnswers.why: counted the shoes, not the pairs
wrongAnswers.remedy: A pair is TWO shoes together. Put them in twos — now count the pairs, not the shoes.

wrongAnswers.why: stopped after the first group
wrongAnswers.remedy: Keep pairing until no shoes are left. How many pairs did you make altogether?

hints: Put the shoes together in 2s.
Count the pairs, not the shoes.

reteach.say: Line up the 4 shoes. Slide them together in twos: that's one pair… and another pair. Two pairs, no shoes left over. 4 ÷ 2 = 2.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave sharing, grouping and fact-family items.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run that item's reteach with the dealing animated one counter at a time (CPA step down), then serve a level-1 item of the same skill.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 4+ correct across levels 2–3 including one sharing, one grouping and one fact linked to multiplication → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'division as sharing and grouping'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'the sharing wasn't one-to-each' / 'we counted the sweets, not the bags' / 'the ÷ turned into a − there'.
Go concrete: deal counters onto plates together, one at a time, chanting the rhythm.
One hint: 'Every plate gets one before any plate gets two.'
Re-ask smaller (6 ÷ 3), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Recast shares with the learner's interests — party bags, football team kits, trading cards between friends (use real friends' names). The one-to-each dealing rule stays in every framing; never change the numbers.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable share (drop to 6 ÷ 3 if needed), then process praise: 'you dealt fairly one-to-each instead of guessing — that's exactly how division works.'

differentiation.support: Deal one-to-each like cards until gone (the KB fix for guessing); keep plates labelled with the friends' names; if real counters are handy at home, dealing along physically is encouraged.
differentiation.stretch: Find BOTH division facts from 4 × 5 = 20; discuss a share that leaves one left over (13 between 4).

extension: Play 'fair dealer' — deal a small deck of cards so every player gets the same; write the division fact you just performed.
assessmentEvidence: Child shares a quantity equally and groups it, gives the correct quotient, and links it to a multiplication fact.
revisitLater: Division feeds fractions of quantities (Lesson 14) directly — ¼ of 12 IS 12 ÷ 4. Quick mixed ÷ items return in Lesson 12's workout.
